slides.title: Merge, and merge again
slides.subtitle: Greedy pair merge · agglomerative clustering
slides.transcript: This module starts from single nodes and each time puts the two closest clusters together. We trace G01’s full path by hand, explain the tie rule, look closely at the original page’s comparator bug, and preview the capacity constraint.

slides.title: The problem
bullets: Input: a weighted undirected graph, a target K, an optional capacity C
Each step: merge the closest legal pair with affinity > 0
Stop: the count reaches K, or no legal positive pair remains
Output: clusters, cut, whether K is reached, stop reason, a record of each step

bullets.text: Never force a merge to reach K, and never undo a merge

slides.transcript: The input is a graph, a target number of clusters K and an optional capacity. Each step merges the closest legal pair. It stops in one of two cases: the count reaches K, or no legal pair with positive affinity remains. In the second case, report honestly that K is not reached.

slides.title: Singletons, K and the affinity between clusters
bullets: Singletons: at the start every node is its own cluster, and cut = all 18 of the weight
Inter-cluster affinity: the total weight of every wire between two clusters
Contraction: wires between the two become inside wires, and parallel wires add up

bullets.text: Every merge lowers the cut by exactly that merge’s affinity

slides.transcript: At the start every node is a cluster of its own, every wire is cut, and the cut is 18. The affinity of two clusters is the total weight of the wires between them. After a merge those wires are inside, so every merge lowers the cut by exactly that merge’s affinity.

slides.title: The selection key and the tie rule
bullets: Selection key (−affinity, members of A, members of B): compare field by field, take the smallest
The first field is negated: higher affinity comes first
Step 1: A–B and D–E are both 5; compare A with D, so A–B
slides.transcript: Each step compares candidates by the selection key: affinity first, higher is better; on a tie, compare member names. At step one, A–B and D–E are both 5, A comes before D, so A–B merges and the cut drops from 18 to 13.

slides.title: Contraction: parallel wires add up
bullets: A and B contract into the supernode AB (the core illustration by the original author, thy031)
AB–C = A–C 1 + B–C 4 = 5
Another tie at 5 with D–E: [A, B] < [D], so AB–C
cut 13 → 8
slides.transcript: Once A and B contract into a supernode, A–C and B–C are two parallel wires to C that add up to 5, tying D–E again. Comparing members [A, B] with [D], AB–C merges, and the cut drops from 13 to 8.

slides.title: The full path: 18 → 13 → 8 → 3
bullets: Step 3: D–E = 5, cut 8 → 3, the count reaches 2: stop
Result: ABC | DE
Remaining cut: C–D 2 + C–E 1 = 3
With K = 3 it stops after step 2: ABC | D | E, cut 8
slides.transcript: Step three merges D–E, the cut drops from 8 to 3, the count reaches 2, and it stops. The result is ABC against DE, and what remains cut is C–D and C–E. With K equal to 3, it stops after step two, at cut 8.

slides.title: The original page’s comparator bug (fixed)
bullets: Original JS: if (!best || cand < best), where cand is an array
JavaScript turns arrays into strings before comparing
"-1,A,C" < "-5,A,B": affinity 1 counts as better
Four settings give 9/16/12/16; correct is 3/8/8/3

bullets.text: Fix: compare field by field; regression tests 10 vs 2, 2.5 vs 2

slides.transcript: The original page’s JavaScript compared arrays with a less-than sign. JavaScript first turns the arrays into strings and compares them character by character, so the string starting with minus 1 sorts before minus 5, and A–C, with affinity 1, looks like the better pair. All four settings came out wrong. The original Python reference is correct. This course compares field by field and adds regression tests for multi-digit and decimal weights.

slides.title: A capacity preview and the stopping state
bullets: Capacity C = 2: AB + C has size 3 > 2, blocked
D–E merges instead; after that AB+C and C+DE are both over capacity
Stop: AB | C | DE, 3 clusters, cut 8
Legal (every cluster ≤ 2) but K = 2 not reached
Capacity 3: the same path as with no capacity
slides.transcript: With capacity 2, step two would add C to AB, making size 3, over the capacity, so it is blocked and D–E merges instead. After that no legal merge remains, and it stops at three clusters, cut 8. The result is legal, but K is not reached.

slides.title: The pseudocode, line by line
bullets: Line 2: stop once the count reaches K
Lines 3–4: list positive candidates, drop those over capacity
Line 5: with no legal candidate, stop and say so
Line 6: compare selection keys field by field
Line 7: contract; the cut drops by that affinity
slides.transcript: In the pseudocode, line two checks whether K is reached; lines three and four list the candidates and drop those over capacity; line five stops when no legal candidate remains; line six compares selection keys field by field; line seven contracts, and the cut drops by that affinity.

slides.title: Common mistakes
bullets: Comparing candidate arrays as strings: step 1 wrongly picks A–C
Forcing an over-capacity merge to reach K
Forgetting to add parallel wires after a contraction: AB–C taken as 4
Seeing cut 3 and assuming greedy is always optimal
slides.transcript: Common mistakes: comparing arrays as strings; forcing an over-capacity merge to reach K; forgetting to add parallel wires after a contraction; and seeing this graph reach cut 3 and concluding that greedy always finds the optimum.

slides.title: Limits and practical meaning
bullets: No backtracking: a wrong early merge cannot be corrected (counterexample in Module 04)
Depends on the score and the tie rule
A naive version checks every cluster pair each step; real tools use a priority queue and local updates
In chip design it often coarsens many cells into fewer clusters, with a limit on cluster area
slides.transcript: Greedy merging never backtracks, so early mistakes cannot be corrected; the next module gives a counterexample. It depends on the score and the tie rule. A naive implementation checks every cluster pair at every step. In chip design, this kind of merging often coarsens a great many cells into fewer clusters first, while limiting each cluster’s area.

slides.title: Summary
lines: Each step merges the closest legal pair; value first, names break ties.
The cut drops by each merge’s affinity; stop at K or when no legal pair remains, and say so.
Next module: capacity takes centre stage. Does it not fit, or did greedy take a wrong turn?
slides.transcript: In summary: each step merges the closest legal pair, value first, names on a tie. Every merge lowers the cut by that merge’s affinity. Stop when K is reached or no legal positive pair remains, and report it honestly. The next module is about capacity: does it simply not fit, or did greedy take a wrong turn?
